Q011180:
## What Genie Code offers for debugging
Genie Code (the Databricks AI coding and data assistant, formerly called Databricks Assistant) works in notebooks, the SQL editor, Lakeflow Pipelines Editor and dashboards. For errors it has two built-in levels of help.
- **Quick Fix** suggests an automatic recommendation for basic errors, such as a misspelled column or a missing keyword. You review it and choose Accept and run.
- **Diagnose Error** analyzes more complex problems, including environment errors, and tries to fix them.
Databricks recommends always reviewing generated code before running it, because it can make mistakes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Full page Genie Code:** a layout for starting and running several chats from a dedicated page. It is a place to work, not a one-click fix for a failing cell.
- ✗ **B. Genie Migrate:** it translates SQL from other warehouse dialects in a migration project. The code here is already Databricks SQL with a typo, so there is nothing to convert.
- ✓ **C. Quick Fix (correct):** a typo in a column name is a basic error, and Quick Fix presents a recommended correction that the analyst can accept and run in place.
- ✗ **D. Genie Ontology:** it supplies business context such as metric definitions and join hints so new SQL is more accurate. It does not repair a failed cell, and it is not what the question describes.

## Key idea
Basic error in a cell, quick accept: Quick Fix; harder or environment errors: Diagnose Error; always review the code.
Q011181:
## Choosing between the two debugging features
Genie Code separates error help by complexity.
- **Quick Fix** handles basic errors such as typos and offers a one-click Accept and run.
- **Diagnose Error** reads the error and the surrounding context and handles more complex cases, including environment errors, then attempts a fix.
Choosing the right one saves time: a typo does not need a deep diagnosis, and an environment failure is not solved by editing one keyword.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Command shortcuts:** they let you prompt Genie Code from within a cell to generate or change code. They are a way to ask, not an error-analysis feature.
- ✓ **B. Diagnose Error (correct):** it is built for errors beyond simple syntax, including environment errors, and it analyzes the failure and tries to repair it.
- ✗ **C. Inline suggestions:** they help while you write new code. They do not read a failed run and explain the error.
- ✗ **D. Quick Fix:** it targets basic errors with a simple recommended edit. Docs assign environment and more complex failures to Diagnose Error, so this does not match the case.

## Key idea
Simple error: Quick Fix; complex or environment error: Diagnose Error.
Q011182:
## What Genie Code reads
Genie Code uses Unity Catalog metadata, meaning table and column names, descriptions and popular data assets, to give personalized answers while you write, debug and run code. It also uses the code you are working with.
Cryptic column names give the assistant little to go on. A comment such as "Net revenue in USD after discounts" on the column lets it choose correctly, and the description is stored once in Unity Catalog, so every user benefits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Renaming the notebook:** a title is not table metadata, helps only that one notebook and does not tell the assistant what the columns mean.
- ✗ **B. Serverless warehouse:** the warehouse runs the SQL after it is generated. It does not change how the assistant understands column meaning.
- ✗ **C. Pasting data:** the assistant already sends relevant context within the user's permissions, and pasting data is unnecessary, risky for sensitive values and does not document the table for others.
- ✓ **D. Descriptions in Unity Catalog (correct):** the assistant draws on table and column descriptions, so documenting the cryptic columns improves results for all users and all surfaces.

## Key idea
Better Unity Catalog metadata (names, descriptions) gives better Genie Code SQL for every user.
Q011183:
## Genie Code and governance
Genie Code is governed by Unity Catalog permissions. It can only access data and perform operations that the signed-in user has permissions for. To complete a task it sends the prompt and relevant context, such as table and column names, descriptions and the code in use, to the model, all within the user's permissions.
So an analyst without SELECT on a finance table will not get content from it, and an administrator does not need a separate policy for the assistant.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. User's Unity Catalog permissions (correct):** the assistant acts with the permissions of the person asking, so it cannot go beyond what that person can already do.
- ✗ **B. Split enforcement:** permissions are not applied differently to metadata and values in this way; the assistant works within what the user is permitted to see.
- ✗ **C. Default catalog only:** access depends on privileges, not on which catalog is the workspace default.
- ✗ **D. Service credential:** there is no broad identity behind the assistant; using one would bypass governance, which the documentation says does not happen.

## Key idea
Genie Code inherits the user's Unity Catalog permissions; it adds no extra access.
Q011184:
## The Genie family
- **Genie Code** is the AI coding and data assistant for developers and technical practitioners. It generates, runs and debugs code in notebooks, the SQL editor, pipelines and dashboards.
- **Genie One** is for business users who want a simplified chat interface to ask data questions, explore dashboards and run apps.
- **Genie Agents (Genie spaces)** are configured by data teams with trusted data, metrics and business rules for a specific domain.
The audience decides which one fits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Genie Code for the analyst and Genie One for business users (correct):** this matches the documented audiences, coding help for technical users and simple chat for business users.
- ✗ **B. Agents for SQL writing:** a Genie space is a curated environment that data teams configure for domain questions. It is not the coding assistant in the editor, and Genie Code is not the business chat.
- ✗ **C. Genie One for the analyst:** it targets simple chat for business users, not authoring and debugging code.
- ✗ **D. One product:** the documentation lists them as separate members of the Genie family with distinct audiences.

## Key idea
Writing and fixing code: Genie Code; business chat: Genie One; curated domain spaces: Genie Agents.
Q011185:
## Treat generated SQL as a draft
The documentation recommends always reviewing code generated by Genie Code before running it, because it can sometimes make mistakes. Typical problems are a join on the wrong key, which duplicates rows, or a filter that drops valid rows.
A good check is to compare row counts and one known total with a trusted source. This keeps the speed benefit and still protects the report.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reject everything:** the output is often a useful draft; the advice is to review it, not to avoid it.
- ✗ **B. Run unchanged:** nothing guarantees the logic matches the business question; passing the schema check does not mean the join keys or filters are right.
- ✗ **C. Run first, compare later:** this puts unchecked numbers in front of readers, so errors would already have been published.
- ✓ **D. Review and test (correct):** the assistant is a productivity tool whose output must be verified, and a sample check catches wrong joins or filters before anyone relies on them.

## Key idea
Review and verify generated SQL before publishing; it is a draft, not a guarantee.
Q011186:
## Three ways to get help
- **Chat** answers questions and writes code from a prompt.
- **Inline suggestions and autocomplete** offer AI-based completions as you type, using Unity Catalog metadata.
- **Quick Fix / Diagnose Error** react to errors after a run.
For typing speed, inline suggestions are the right fit; no prompt or failed run is involved.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Diagnose Error:** it reacts to an error that has already occurred, so it cannot help while a new statement is being written.
- ✗ **B. Chat:** it needs a question typed into the chat pane, which the analyst wants to avoid.
- ✓ **C. Inline suggestions and autocomplete (correct):** they present AI-based completions in the editor as the analyst types, with no chat prompt.
- ✗ **D. Searched documentation:** it is the step shown when Genie Code answers from Databricks documentation, not a code completion.

## Key idea
Typing help: inline suggestions; errors: Quick Fix or Diagnose Error; questions: chat.
Q011187:
## Matching tools to tasks
Genie Code is integrated into notebooks and the SQL editor. It sees the code you are working with, plus Unity Catalog metadata, and can explain or fix it.
A Genie space answers business questions over curated datasets in natural language; it is not an editor assistant. Query history lists past executions for review, and alerts watch query results against a threshold. Neither repairs code.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Query history:** it records what ran, which helps in review and analysis, but it does not correct statements.
- ✓ **B. Genie Code (correct):** it is the assistant that works on the code in the notebook, including error diagnosis and fixes.
- ✗ **C. Genie space:** spaces answer data questions on trusted datasets for consumers. They do not edit notebook cells.
- ✗ **D. Scheduled alert:** alerts evaluate a query against a condition and notify. They do not change code.

## Key idea
Fixing code in an editor: Genie Code; asking curated data questions: Genie space.
Q011188:
## Compute versus storage versus governance
- **Data** lives in cloud storage and is registered as Unity Catalog tables.
- **Governance** (who can read which table, column or row) comes from Unity Catalog privileges.
- **Compute** is what runs the query. In Databricks SQL that is a **SQL warehouse**, a compute resource that lets you query and explore data.
The SQL editor, Catalog Explorer and dashboards each pick a warehouse from a compute drop-down.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replacing privileges:** Unity Catalog governs data access; the warehouse has its own ACL for who can use it, but that does not grant column access.
- ✓ **B. Compute that executes the query (correct):** the warehouse runs the SQL, while storage holds the data and Unity Catalog governs access.
- ✗ **C. Building dashboards:** a dashboard is built by a user on top of datasets; a warehouse does not convert result sets into one.
- ✗ **D. Storing data:** warehouses are compute; table files remain in cloud storage under Unity Catalog and do not live in the warehouse.

## Key idea
SQL warehouse = the compute that runs Databricks SQL; Unity Catalog = governance; cloud storage = the data.
Q011189:
## Warehouse auto-start
A SQL warehouse auto-restarts when a query is run against it while stopped, when a job assigned to it is scheduled, when a JDBC/ODBC connection is made, or when a dashboard tied to it is opened. Users need the right permission on the warehouse (Can use to run queries).
Auto stop saves cost when nobody is querying; auto start keeps this transparent for analysts. Serverless warehouses start much faster than other types.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Local engine:** the SQL editor has no local engine; SQL always executes on a SQL warehouse.
- ✗ **B. Random other warehouse:** queries run on the warehouse the user selected, not on one picked by the workspace.
- ✓ **C. Automatic start (correct):** running a query on a stopped warehouse starts it if the user has access, so the query runs after the startup delay.
- ✗ **D. Administrator must start:** manual start is possible for people with Can monitor or more, but it is not required, since a query triggers auto-start.

## Key idea
A query on a stopped warehouse auto-starts it for users with access.
Q011190:
## Size answers "one query is heavy", cluster count answers "many queries at once"
A SQL warehouse has a **cluster size** (for example Medium or Large) and, for concurrency, a minimum and maximum number of clusters.
- Larger size gives one cluster more memory and cores. The documentation advises increasing the size when queries spill to disk, which you can see in the query profile.
- More clusters let the warehouse admit more queries at once. They do not make a single query bigger.
Here nothing is queued, so concurrency is not the problem. Serverless is also the warehouse type that handles queuing best, so a classic type would not help.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Larger cluster size (correct):** spilling means one cluster lacks memory for this query, and a bigger size provides more memory and compute for it.
- ✗ **B. More clusters:** extra clusters serve concurrent queries, while one query runs on one cluster, so the spill remains. Nothing is queued here anyway.
- ✗ **C. Classic type:** classic has Photon only and none of the serverless performance features, so it does not remove spilling and it starts slower.
- ✗ **D. Second warehouse:** running the query twice doubles the cost and each copy still spills, because each runs on a cluster of the same size.

## Key idea
Spilling in the query profile: increase cluster size; queueing under many users: raise the maximum clusters.
Q011191:
## Size versus number of clusters
For classic and pro warehouses you pick a **cluster size** and a **minimum and maximum number of clusters**.
- Cluster size mainly speeds up a single query (more memory and cores).
- The number of clusters governs **concurrency**. Autoscaling adds clusters based on the estimated time to process running and queued queries, and Databricks suggests about one cluster per 10 concurrent queries.
Queueing with fast individual queries is a concurrency problem, so raise the maximum clusters.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Materialized view:** it may help specific heavy queries, but it does not answer the stated problem of many concurrent users waiting.
- ✗ **B. Disabling Photon:** Photon speeds up queries and does not restrict admission, so turning it off would not reduce queueing.
- ✗ **C. Larger size only:** size accelerates a single query; it is not the main lever for concurrent users, and fast queries show size is not the issue.
- ✓ **D. More clusters (correct):** queueing under concurrent load is addressed by letting autoscaling add clusters, up to a higher maximum.

## Key idea
Queueing at peak: raise the maximum number of clusters; slow single queries: increase size.
Q011192:
## Two permission layers
- **Unity Catalog privileges** (such as SELECT) govern the data.
- **SQL warehouse ACLs** govern the compute: Can view lets users see warehouses, query history and profiles but not run queries; **Can use** lets users run queries; Can monitor adds monitoring for tuning; Can manage controls the warehouse itself.
An analyst needs both a data privilege and a warehouse permission.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Account admin:** nothing requires administrator rights to run queries; the permission is granted at warehouse level.
- ✗ **B. Catalog ownership:** owning a catalog governs data objects, not the right to use compute.
- ✗ **C. Can view:** it lets users view warehouses and history, but they cannot run queries, so it is the wrong level.
- ✓ **D. Can use (correct):** it is the permission for users who need to run queries on the warehouse; data access via SELECT already exists.

## Key idea
Running queries needs data privileges (Unity Catalog) plus Can use on the warehouse.
Q011193:
## Query federation
Query federation lets you run queries against external relational databases through JDBC. You create a **connection** to the database and a **foreign catalog** in Unity Catalog that mirrors it. Its tables then appear with three-level names, for example `pg_cat.public.customers`, and you can join them with Delta tables:
`SELECT ... FROM sales.orders o JOIN pg_cat.public.customers c ON o.cust_id = c.id`
Access is governed by Unity Catalog, and parts of the query are pushed down to the remote database.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Connection plus foreign catalog (correct):** this is query federation, which queries the database in place under Unity Catalog governance and joins with Delta tables.
- ✗ **B. Delta Sharing:** sharing is a protocol for exchanging data between Delta or Unity Catalog parties, not a way to expose a PostgreSQL database.
- ✗ **C. CSV export and upload:** it creates a stale copy that needs repeating, and the question asks to query in place.
- ✗ **D. Convert to PostgreSQL:** Delta tables are not moved into the remote database for the join; federation joins them on the Databricks side.

## Key idea
Join Delta with an external relational database in place: connection and foreign catalog (query federation).
Q011194:
## Federated queries are written in Spark SQL
A foreign catalog exposes remote tables, but the SQL that the analyst writes is Databricks SQL. The documentation for foreign catalogs states that queries must use **Apache Spark data types**, and each connector page lists how Spark types map to the types of the external database. For example, a PostgreSQL `numeric(12,2)` column is read as a Spark `DECIMAL(12,2)`.
So the analyst writes `CAST(order_total AS DECIMAL(12,2))`, and Databricks translates it when it pushes work to the source.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. OPTIMIZE:** this compacts Delta files; a remote table has none, and it does not change data types in a query.
- ✗ **B. MODIFY grant:** the foreign table is read-only and the failure is a type error, not a missing privilege.
- ✓ **C. Spark data types (correct):** the query is Databricks SQL, so casts must use Spark types, and the connector maps them to the PostgreSQL types.
- ✗ **D. Pro warehouse:** the warehouse type does not change the SQL dialect of the query, so remote type names are rejected on every type.

## Key idea
Federated queries use Spark SQL and Spark data types, not the remote database's type names.
Q011195:
## Setting up query federation
Query federation needs two Unity Catalog objects, created in this order.
- A **connection** that stores the access credentials and the JDBC URL of the external database.
- A **foreign catalog** created from that connection, which mirrors the database.
Then privileges on the foreign tables are granted to users, and their queries are pushed down to the external database. The external location and storage credential belong to catalog federation, where queries read object storage directly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Grants first:** there are no foreign tables to grant on until the catalog exists.
- ✓ **B. Connection, foreign catalog, grants, queries (correct):** the foreign catalog is created from the connection, and privileges can be granted only on objects that exist.
- ✗ **C. Storage steps and ingestion:** this is the catalog federation setup for files in object storage, followed by a copy, and it is not query federation, which queries the database live.
- ✗ **D. Catalog first:** a foreign catalog is created using a connection, so the connection has to exist first.

## Key idea
Query federation: connection, then foreign catalog, then grants, then queries.
Q011196:
## Foreign catalog details
A foreign catalog is a securable object in Unity Catalog that mirrors a database in an external system. In Catalog Explorer it looks like other catalogs, with owner, privileges and schemas, and it adds the **connection** it uses and the external database or catalog it mirrors.
The connection holds the JDBC URL and the credentials. Analysts see which connection is used, but they do not receive the secret itself; they query through Unity Catalog with their own privileges.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Name only:** Catalog Explorer shows the same details as for standard catalogs and in addition the connection and the mirrored database.
- ✓ **B. Standard details plus connection and mirrored database (correct):** this is how the docs describe Catalog Explorer for a foreign catalog, so the analyst can see where the data comes from.
- ✗ **C. Delta copy:** federation keeps no copy; the tables are read from the source when queried.
- ✗ **D. Plain-text credentials:** credentials stay in the connection and are not displayed to analysts, which is what keeps central auditing possible.

## Key idea
Foreign catalog in Catalog Explorer: standard catalog details plus the connection and the external database it mirrors.
Q011197:
## Materialize a heavy federated result
Federation reads the source live, so each query puts work on the remote database. When the same expensive result is read often, the analyst can precompute it.
- A **materialized view** can be created on external data through Lakehouse Federation. It stores the result as a managed table and refreshes on a schedule or trigger, so dashboard viewers read the stored table.
- The remote database then sees one refresh instead of one query per viewer.
For very large volumes or low latency, Databricks recommends Lakeflow Connect ingestion instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Materialized view (correct):** the aggregation runs once per refresh against PostgreSQL, and every dashboard open reads the stored result.
- ✗ **B. Dedicated warehouses:** more compute on the Databricks side does not remove the repeated queries sent to the source, and each viewer would run the same work.
- ✗ **C. Managed catalog:** a foreign catalog cannot be converted, and the source data would still need to be copied to Delta first.
- ✗ **D. Standard view:** it stores nothing and re-runs the full federated query each time, so the load on PostgreSQL remains.

## Key idea
Same heavy federated result read by many: materialize it; foreign tables themselves stay read-only.
Q011198:
## Hiding sensitive data in a materialized view
A materialized view stores its result, but it can still protect columns and rows. The documentation describes two ways.
- Leave the sensitive column out of the query.
- Use `MASK` for columns and `ROW FILTER` for rows when creating the view, so the output depends on the permissions of the user who queries. For example, the `tax_id` column can be hidden for users outside a group.
A mask function typically calls `is_account_group_member()`, the same function that dynamic views use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Classic warehouse:** the warehouse type has nothing to do with column visibility; masks and grants control it.
- ✗ **B. One refresh per group:** a materialized view has one stored result, and multiple copies would multiply storage and refresh work.
- ✗ **C. Temporary:** a materialized view is a Unity Catalog managed table, and it cannot be made session-only to protect a column.
- ✓ **D. Column mask on the materialized view (correct):** the stored table is the same for all, and the mask decides at read time what each group sees.

## Key idea
Protect columns or rows of a materialized view with MASK and ROW FILTER, based on the querying user's group.
Q011199:
## What a refresh of a streaming table processes
A streaming table keeps state about what it has already read, so each row is handled once. When `REFRESH` runs, it processes the data available from the sources at the start of the run. New data that is added to the sources during the run is ignored until the next refresh.
The analyst does not lose these files. Running another refresh, or defining a `SCHEDULE` or `TRIGGER ON UPDATE` for the table, brings them in.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Silent failure:** nothing is broken, and the table continues from where it stopped, so no recreate is needed.
- ✗ **B. Only files at creation:** each refresh reads new files, since the table processes a growing dataset incrementally.
- ✓ **C. Start-of-run snapshot (correct):** files that landed during the refresh are left for the next refresh, which processes them once.
- ✗ **D. Materialized view in between:** streaming tables read their sources directly, and no other object is needed.

## Key idea
A streaming table refresh processes data available at its start; later arrivals wait for the next refresh.
Q011200:
## Dynamic views
A dynamic view is a regular view whose query uses functions that depend on the user: `session_user()` for the email, `is_account_group_member()` for account-level groups (recommended for Unity Catalog data), while `is_member()` checks only workspace groups and is not recommended.
Example: `CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('auditors') THEN email ELSE 'REDACTED' END AS email`.
Nothing is stored; the logic runs on every query. Grant users access to the view, not to the underlying table.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Dynamic view (correct):** one view, evaluated per user on each query, shows real emails to auditors and masks them for everyone else without duplicating data.
- ✗ **B. Streaming table:** it is an ingestion object that processes rows once; it does not decide output per reader.
- ✗ **C. Materialized view per group:** it stores copies, which the team wants to avoid, and one stored result cannot vary by the reader.
- ✗ **D. Temporary view:** it exists only in a session and does not provide shared governance for other analysts.

## Key idea
Different results by who queries, without copies: dynamic view.
Q011201:
## Where the work happens
- **Dynamic view**: a view that applies user-based logic (group membership, current user) when the query runs. No data is stored; use it for row and column level protection.
- **Materialized view**: a managed table that stores query results and refreshes them, used for performance.
The first is about who sees what at read time; the second is about precomputing for speed. They can be combined, but they solve different problems.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Source requirements:** neither type needs those sources; a dynamic view is defined on ordinary tables and a materialized view on Delta or other supported tables.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Dynamic view computes at query time and can vary by user; materialized view stores precomputed results and is refreshed.
- ✗ **C. Reversed:** this swaps the two definitions. The dynamic view stores nothing.
- ✗ **D. Access restriction:** view access follows grants and not ownership alone, and materialized views are governed by Unity Catalog too, not open to everyone.

## Key idea
Dynamic view = per-user logic at read time; materialized view = stored, refreshed results.
Q011202:
## Refresh options
A materialized view can refresh by a **cron schedule** (`SCHEDULE CRON ...`), **on trigger** (`TRIGGER ON UPDATE`, refreshes whenever the upstream source data changes), or manually with `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`. Databricks says to use trigger-based refresh for production workloads, especially when upstream dependencies don't run on predictable schedules.
Refresh may be incremental (only changed data) or full; a cost model chooses by default.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Temporary view:** it stores no results, so it would re-run the full query on every read instead of precomputing.
- ✗ **B. Daily cron early:** a fixed time either runs before late loads and shows stale data, or wastes work if the data arrives sooner.
- ✗ **C. Manual refresh:** this relies on memory and defeats automation for a recurring report.
- ✓ **D. TRIGGER ON UPDATE (correct):** the view refreshes after the source changes, which fits loads at unpredictable times and avoids a fixed schedule.

## Key idea
Unpredictable upstream timing: TRIGGER ON UPDATE; known timing: cron schedule.
Q011203:
## A dynamic view protects only what goes through it
A dynamic view hides data by running user-dependent logic, such as `is_account_group_member()`, whenever someone queries the view. The base table itself is not changed. Anyone who has `SELECT` on the table can read the table directly and see every value.
Databricks recommends not granting users the ability to read the tables and views that the dynamic view references. Give the analysts privileges on the view only, plus the usage privileges on its catalog and schema.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. is_member():** that function checks workspace groups only and is not recommended for Unity Catalog data; it does not stop direct table reads either.
- ✗ **B. Rows only:** dynamic views handle security at the level of columns or rows, with masking as an example.
- ✓ **C. Remove direct table access (correct):** the masking logic lives only in the view, so users must be allowed to read the view and not the base table.
- ✗ **D. Materialized view:** it stores a result and would not change who can read the base table.

## Key idea
Dynamic view works only if users are granted the view and not the base table.
Q011204:
## How a standalone materialized view runs
When you create a materialized view in a Databricks SQL warehouse, a serverless pipeline is created to process the create and the refreshes. You do not manage that compute. You can monitor refresh status in Catalog Explorer (for example the details shown by `DESCRIBE EXTENDED`), and you can start one with `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`.
Creation itself blocks until the view is created and loaded.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Serverless pipeline (correct):** Databricks runs creation and refreshes on a managed serverless pipeline, and the analyst reviews refresh status in Catalog Explorer.
- ✗ **B. Laptop:** processing runs in Databricks compute; nothing executes on a client machine.
- ✗ **C. Only on dashboard open:** refreshes follow the schedule, trigger or manual command, not dashboard views, and their status is recorded.
- ✗ **D. Classic cluster:** no cluster is needed from the analyst; a serverless pipeline handles the work.

## Key idea
SQL-warehouse-created materialized views refresh through a serverless pipeline; check status in Catalog Explorer.
Q011205:
## On demand versus precomputed
- A **standard view** is a saved query. Every read runs the full query against the underlying tables, so it always sees current data but pays full cost each time.
- A **materialized view** stores the result as a managed table. Reads are fast because the work is done at refresh time, and the data is as fresh as the last refresh.
Choose a standard view for freshness and simplicity, a materialized view for repeated expensive queries.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reversed roles:** this swaps the two behaviors. A standard view stores nothing and recomputes on every read, while a materialized view holds the stored result.
- ✗ **B. Source requirements:** views do not depend on streaming or external catalogs; both work on ordinary tables.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Standard view is computed on demand; materialized view stores results and refreshes them, trading some freshness for speed.
- ✗ **D. Refresh claim:** standard views have nothing to refresh, and materialized views do need refreshes by schedule, trigger or command.

## Key idea
Standard view = compute each read; materialized view = stored result, refreshed.
